case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Eighth Amendment's Cruel and Unusual Punishment Clause prohibits cities from enforcing public camping ordinances against homeless individuals when there is no adequate shelter available.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Eighth Amendment to the United States Constitution (Cruel and Unusual Punishment Clause), specifically as applied to municipal anti-camping and public sleeping ordinances enacted by the City of Grants Pass, Oregon.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The City of Grants Pass argues that its public camping ordinances are constitutionally valid regulations of public conduct, not punishments targeting the status of being homeless. The city contends that the Ninth Circuit's reliance on Martin v. City of Boise misread Supreme Court precedent by improperly extending the Eighth Amendment to bar enforcement of neutral public order laws, leaving local governments without clear guidance on how to manage homeless encampments and creating an unworkable population-level inquiry that hamstrings municipalities from addressing a serious public crisis. The city further argues the ruling creates an irreconcilable conflict with the California Supreme Court's decision in Tobe v. City of Santa Ana, subjecting law enforcement officers to contradictory legal obligations depending on which court system adjudicates a given dispute.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that the Ninth Circuit correctly applied Supreme Court precedent because the ordinances deliberately target and discriminate against a vulnerable socioeconomic class of homeless individuals, effectively criminalizing innocent and involuntary acts — such as sleeping outdoors — that are necessary for survival when no shelter alternatives exist. Respondents contend that the Eighth Amendment's substantive limits on what conduct can be criminalized, as recognized in Robinson v. California and Powell v. Texas, prohibit punishing individuals for conduct that is an unavoidable consequence of their status or condition. They further assert that enforcing these ordinances constitutes grossly disproportionate punishment and violates the founders' original intent in adopting the Cruel and Unusual Punishment Clause.
key_precedents: Martin v. City of Boise, 920 F.3d 584 (9th Cir. 2019)
Tobe v. City of Santa Ana, 9 Cal. 4th 1069 (1995)
Auto Equity Sales, Inc. v. Superior Court, 57 Cal. 2d 450 (1962)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor's argument — that punishing conduct inseparable from an involuntary condition collapses the act/status distinction — is the strongest challenge to our position, but it founders on the Powell plurality's explicit refusal to constitutionalize that very theory, and as Justice Kagan correctly notes, accepting it would produce a rule with no limiting principle. My minimalist instincts actually counsel in favor of the Petitioner here: the narrowest defensible reading of Robinson cabins it to pure status crimes, and the Ninth Circuit's population-level shelter-availability inquiry is precisely the kind of unworkable, sweeping constitutional mandate that courts should avoid when democratic processes remain available. As Chief Justice, I would assign a majority opinion that reverses on the narrow ground that Grants Pass's ordinances regulate conduct rather than status, explicitly declining to overrule Robinson or address whether any conduct-based Eighth Amendment protection could ever exist — preserving the question Justice White's Powell concurrence raised without resolving it. This narrow holding respects institutional legitimacy, leaves open future as-applied challenges under other constitutional provisions (due process, equal protection), and avoids constitutionalizing the entire field of homelessness policy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor presents the strongest argument for the respondents — that punishing conduct inseparable from an involuntary condition effectively punishes status — but this reasoning proves too much and was explicitly rejected by the Powell plurality, which recognized that accepting such logic would constitutionalize vast swaths of criminal law with no limiting principle, as Justice Marshall himself warned. The original public meaning of the Eighth Amendment, as confirmed by Ingraham v. Wright, directed the Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause at the method and kind of punishment, not at the substantive legislative authority to define criminal conduct; there is simply no historical evidence that the Framers understood this provision to strip governments of their police power to regulate public spaces. Justice Gorsuch correctly identifies the separation of powers problem at the heart of the Ninth Circuit's rule — transforming federal courts into administrators of municipal homeless policy through an unworkable population-level shelter-availability inquiry that no majority of this Court has ever endorsed and that finds no grounding in constitutional text or history. Even accepting Robinson as binding precedent for the narrow proposition that pure status cannot be criminalized, Grants Pass's ordinances plainly regulate conduct — the act of camping in public spaces — not the status of being homeless, and the act/status distinction, however imperfect philosophically, is the only workable line the Constitution's text and our precedents can support.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor presents the strongest opposing argument — that punishing conduct inseparable from an involuntary condition collapses the act/status distinction — but this reasoning proves too much and lacks any limiting principle, precisely the concern Justice Marshall articulated in Powell. If biological necessity transforms conduct into status for Eighth Amendment purposes, then virtually any conduct flowing from poverty, addiction, or mental illness becomes constitutionally immune from regulation, a result no majority of this Court has ever endorsed and one that would constitutionalize vast swaths of criminal law. The Ninth Circuit's shelter-availability inquiry illustrates exactly how unworkable this framework becomes in practice: municipalities cannot enforce neutral public order laws without first conducting a jurisdiction-wide census of shelter beds, an obligation with no textual or historical grounding in the Eighth Amendment. I am reinforced in my position by Justice Kagan's acknowledgment — notable given her general sympathies — that the doctrinal line must hold at Robinson's status/act distinction, and by Justice Thomas's correct observation that the original public meaning of the Clause was directed at methods of punishment, not substantive legislative authority to define criminal conduct.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Kagan's limiting principle argument is the most formidable challenge to my position, and I respect her reasoning deeply — but I remain unpersuaded that Powell forecloses this case, because Powell involved a defendant who had access to treatment and whose conduct (public intoxication) was not the literal biological minimum for survival. The limiting principle I would draw is narrow: the Eighth Amendment bars criminalization only when (1) the conduct is a biological necessity for survival, (2) no legal alternative exists, and (3) the condition causing the conduct is involuntary — sleep satisfies all three in a way that addiction-driven conduct in Powell did not. Justice Jackson's point about equal protection and due process as alternative remedies is well-taken, and I would acknowledge in dissent that those doctrines may provide overlapping protection, but the Eighth Amendment's core anti-degradation principle — which Robinson itself embodies — is directly implicated when government uses criminal law to punish people for the inescapable physical consequences of poverty. I write to preserve this constitutional argument for future development, recognizing that the majority's concerns about workability deserve serious weight in remedy design even if they do not defeat the underlying constitutional claim.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor raises the most compelling argument for the respondents — that when conduct is the inescapable biological consequence of an involuntary condition, punishing it collapses into punishing the status itself. I take this seriously, and it is the argument that gives me the most pause. But as Justice Jackson notes, Powell v. Texas directly confronted this logic and declined to extend Robinson even to conduct closely tied to a condition, and Justice Marshall's plurality opinion explicitly warned that any such extension would lack a limiting principle — a concern fully vindicated by the Ninth Circuit's unworkable population-level shelter-availability inquiry. The Eighth Amendment's text and historical application, as Ingraham v. Wright confirms, have been directed at the method of punishment, not at defining the outer limits of criminalized conduct; the status/act distinction, however imperfect at the margins, remains the only judicially manageable line Robinson drew. While I share Justice Sotomayor's deep concern for homeless individuals subjected to these ordinances, the proper constitutional instruments for addressing this crisis are equal protection, due process, and the democratic process — not an expansion of the Cruel and Unusual Punishment Clause that would constitutionalize a vast and unmanageable swath of criminal law.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor presents the strongest opposing argument — that when conduct is the inescapable biological consequence of an involuntary condition, punishing that conduct is functionally indistinguishable from punishing the status itself. This is a serious argument, but it founders on two grounds under my methodology. First, the text and original public meaning of the Eighth Amendment simply do not support reading 'cruel and unusual punishments' as a substantive constraint on what conduct legislatures may criminalize; the Clause speaks to the nature of punishment imposed, not to the threshold question of criminalization. Second, and critically, Powell v. Texas directly confronted this 'involuntary conduct' argument and rejected it — Justice Marshall's plurality recognized that accepting it would dissolve any limiting principle, a concern Justice Kagan rightly emphasizes is fully realized in the Ninth Circuit's shelter-availability inquiry, which has no manageable stopping point and would constitutionalize vast swaths of criminal law. The proper constitutional instruments for addressing the genuine humanitarian concerns Justice Sotomayor raises are equal protection, due process, and above all the democratic branches — not a judicially manufactured Eighth Amendment rule that transforms federal courts into administrators of municipal homeless policy with no textual warrant.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor presents the strongest counterargument — that when no shelter exists, sleeping outdoors becomes the inescapable consequence of homelessness itself, collapsing the act/status distinction Robinson drew. But as Justice Kagan correctly identifies, this reasoning has no limiting principle: if biological necessity transforms conduct into status for Eighth Amendment purposes, then virtually any survival behavior — eating, drinking, existing in public — could be constitutionalized, stripping legislatures of authority that Powell v. Texas explicitly preserved. The Powell plurality's refusal to extend Robinson to conduct, even involuntary conduct, was not an oversight but a deliberate recognition that the judiciary lacks the institutional competence to manage the cascading consequences of such a rule — consequences fully realized in the Ninth Circuit's unworkable population-level shelter-availability inquiry. My institutionalist commitments reinforce this conclusion: constitutionalizing homelessness policy through the Eighth Amendment would entangle federal courts in municipal governance without textual warrant, undermining both the Court's legitimacy and the democratic processes better suited to address this genuine human crisis.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor presents the strongest opposing argument — that when no shelter exists, sleeping outdoors becomes the inescapable biological consequence of homelessness, collapsing the status/conduct distinction Robinson drew. But as Justice Kagan correctly identifies, this reasoning lacks any limiting principle: if involuntary conduct inseparable from a condition is constitutionally protected from criminalization, then virtually any conduct compelled by circumstance or condition could claim Eighth Amendment shelter, which Justice Marshall himself warned against in Powell. The text and original public meaning of the Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause, as confirmed by Ingraham v. Wright, directed the provision at the method and kind of punishment imposed following conviction — not at the substantive legislative authority to define criminal conduct — and Grants Pass's ordinances plainly regulate the act of camping in public spaces, not the status of being homeless. While I am genuinely troubled by the human consequences of enforcing these ordinances against individuals with nowhere to go, the proper constitutional instruments for addressing that concern are equal protection, due process, and the democratic process — not an Eighth Amendment doctrine that would transform federal courts into administrators of municipal shelter policy with no workable limiting principle.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor's biological necessity argument remains the most powerful challenge to our position, and I want to be transparent that it genuinely troubles me — my experience as a public defender leaves me acutely aware that these ordinances function as instruments of systematic harassment against people who have nowhere else to go. But Justice Kagan's limiting principle concern, reinforced by Powell's explicit rejection of the involuntary-conduct theory, is ultimately decisive: once we accept that conduct inseparable from an involuntary condition cannot be criminalized, we have no principled basis to confine that rule to sleep and homelessness rather than extending it to public intoxication by alcoholics, drug use by addicts, or any survival behavior compelled by poverty or mental illness. The Ninth Circuit's population-level shelter-availability inquiry perfectly illustrates the unworkability problem — it transforms federal courts into administrators of municipal housing policy with no textual warrant and no manageable stopping point. I write separately to emphasize that equal protection and due process doctrines remain robust tools for challenging pretextual or discriminatory enforcement, and that the democratic branches — through shelter funding, housing-first policies, and decriminalization — are both the constitutionally appropriate and practically more effective remedies for the genuine human crisis Justice Sotomayor rightly identifies.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Eighth Amendment's Cruel and Unusual Punishment Clause, as interpreted in Powell v. Texas, prohibits punishment of mere status but does not extend to bar enforcement of neutral public conduct regulations, even where that conduct may be linked to a condition or circumstance. The plurality in Powell explicitly declined to extend Robinson v. California's status-crime prohibition to involuntary conduct flowing from status, and only four Justices have ever endorsed even Justice White's narrower concurrence suggesting some conduct-based protection — meaning no majority of this Court has ever held that the Eighth Amendment constrains what conduct may be criminalized beyond pure status offenses. The Ninth Circuit's Martin framework creates an unworkable, population-level inquiry that strips municipalities of their traditional police powers to regulate public spaces, implicates serious federalism concerns, and rests on a constitutional foundation that lacks majority support in our precedents. Consistent with my commitment to narrow rulings and institutional legitimacy, I would reverse the Ninth Circuit and leave to the democratic process — not the Eighth Amendment — the difficult policy questions surrounding homelessness, shelter availability, and public order.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The original public meaning of the Eighth Amendment's Cruel and Unusual Punishment Clause, as understood at ratification, was directed exclusively at the method and kind of punishment imposed by courts following criminal conviction — not at constraining the substantive legislative authority of governments to define criminal conduct. Robinson v. California was a dramatic and historically unsupported departure from this original understanding, and Powell v. Texas wisely refused to extend it further. The Ninth Circuit's reliance on Martin v. City of Boise improperly extended Robinson's already-dubious holding to bar enforcement of facially neutral public order ordinances, effectively stripping municipalities of their traditional police power to regulate public spaces — a power firmly rooted in the constitutional structure of federalism and reserved to the states. As Ingraham v. Wright confirms, the Eighth Amendment has 'always been considered, and properly so, to be directed at the method or kind of punishment imposed for the violation of criminal statutes,' not at the threshold legislative decision of what conduct to criminalize.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Eighth Amendment's Cruel and Unusual Punishment Clause, properly understood through its text and original meaning, restricts how punishment may be imposed, not what conduct legislatures may criminalize. Robinson v. California's narrow holding prohibits punishing mere status — being an addict — but the Powell plurality explicitly refused to extend this principle to conduct, even conduct allegedly flowing 'involuntarily' from a status, reaffirming the act/status distinction that forecloses the Ninth Circuit's reasoning. The Ninth Circuit improperly stitched together a Powell dissent and a single Justice's dicta to manufacture a binding rule that no majority of this Court has ever endorsed — a methodological error that Marks v. United States itself would not sanction, since Justice White's concurrence cannot be reconciled with the plurality on a common rationale. Grants Pass's ordinances regulate public conduct — camping and sleeping in public spaces — not the status of being homeless, and permitting cities to enforce neutral public order laws against such conduct is fully consistent with precedent and essential to allowing municipalities to address a serious public safety and health crisis without being paralyzed by an unworkable shelter-availability inquiry.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Robinson v. California established that the Eighth Amendment prohibits criminalizing status, and when a city enforces anti-camping ordinances against individuals who have no access to shelter, it effectively punishes the unavoidable conduct inseparable from the status of homelessness itself — a distinction that collapses under these circumstances. While Powell v. Texas declined to extend Robinson to public intoxication, that plurality decision did not foreclose the principle that punishing conduct which is the inescapable consequence of an involuntary condition crosses the constitutional line Robinson drew. The practical reality — which my judicial philosophy demands I confront — is that homeless individuals forced to sleep outdoors are not making a voluntary lifestyle choice but are responding to a biological necessity, and fining or jailing them for that necessity when no shelter bed exists is grossly disproportionate and serves no legitimate penological purpose beyond harassment of a vulnerable population. Grants Pass's ordinances, as applied to individuals with no shelter alternative, therefore constitute cruel and unusual punishment under the Eighth Amendment, consistent with the Ninth Circuit's reasoning in Martin v. City of Boise.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Powell plurality's refusal to extend Robinson beyond status crimes to involuntary conduct is controlling here — Justice Marshall explicitly warned that such an extension would lack 'any limiting principle,' and that concern is fully realized in the Ninth Circuit's unworkable population-level shelter-availability inquiry that leaves municipalities without clear guidance. The Eighth Amendment's Cruel and Unusual Punishment Clause has historically been directed at the method or kind of punishment imposed, not at defining the outer limits of what conduct legislatures may criminalize, and Grants Pass's ordinances punish conduct — camping in public spaces — not the status of being homeless. While I am deeply sympathetic to the respondents' position that enforcing these ordinances against individuals with nowhere else to go raises serious constitutional concerns, the doctrinal line must be drawn at Robinson's status/act distinction; extending it further to involuntary conduct would constitutionalize a vast swath of criminal law with no principled stopping point, displacing democratic and administrative solutions that are better suited to address the homelessness crisis. Cities retain the obligation to pursue humane policies, but the Eighth Amendment is not the proper constitutional instrument to mandate shelter availability or override neutral public-order regulations.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: As a textualist and originalist, I must follow the Eighth Amendment's original public meaning, which — as Ingraham v. Wright confirms — directed the Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause at the 'method or kind of punishment imposed for the violation of criminal statutes,' not at the substantive authority of legislatures to define what conduct is criminal. Robinson v. California carved out a narrow exception prohibiting criminalization of pure status, but Grants Pass's ordinances regulate conduct — the act of camping or sleeping in public spaces — not the status of being homeless, a distinction Powell v. Texas reinforced by refusing to extend Robinson to conduct even when that conduct is compelled by condition. The Ninth Circuit's population-level 'adequate shelter' inquiry has no grounding in the constitutional text, its original meaning, or any manageable limiting principle, and effectively transforms federal courts into administrators of municipal homeless policy — a profound separation of powers problem that leaves local governments without workable guidance. Because the ordinances punish conduct rather than status, and because the historical record provides no support for reading the Eighth Amendment as a substantive constraint on what acts legislatures may criminalize beyond the narrow Robinson status exception, the City of Grants Pass must prevail.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Ninth Circuit's extension of Robinson v. California to bar enforcement of neutral public camping ordinances represents a fundamental category error that neither Robinson nor the fractured Powell v. Texas decision supports. Robinson prohibited criminalizing the mere status of addiction, but as the Powell plurality made clear, punishing conduct — even conduct arguably connected to a status — is constitutionally distinct; the homeless individuals here are being cited for the act of public camping, not for the status of being homeless. The Ninth Circuit's rule creates an unworkable population-level inquiry requiring municipalities to assess shelter availability across an entire jurisdiction before enforcing any public order law, a standard with no grounding in the Eighth Amendment's historical meaning or this Court's precedents and one that severely undermines local governments' practical ability to manage public spaces. Consistent with my emphasis on judicial restraint, historical tradition, and workability, I would reverse the Ninth Circuit and hold that the Cruel and Unusual Punishment Clause does not categorically bar enforcement of facially neutral anti-camping ordinances, leaving policy solutions to the democratic branches where they belong.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: As an originalist and textualist, I must examine what the Eighth Amendment's Cruel and Unusual Punishment Clause meant at the time of ratification, and the historical evidence strongly indicates it was understood as a constraint on the manner and proportionality of punishment — not as a substantive limit on legislative power to define criminal conduct. Robinson v. California, while precedent, represents a significant doctrinal departure from the Amendment's original public meaning, and Powell v. Texas wisely declined to extend Robinson's status/conduct distinction further, with a plurality recognizing the dangers of constitutionalizing what are fundamentally policy questions about criminal liability. Grants Pass's ordinances regulate conduct — camping and sleeping in public spaces — not the status of being homeless, and the Ninth Circuit's population-level 'adequate shelter' inquiry has no textual or historical grounding in the Eighth Amendment and creates an unworkable standard that effectively strips municipalities of their traditional police powers to regulate public spaces. Even accepting Robinson as binding precedent, its holding is properly cabined to the criminalization of pure status, and extending it to compel cities to demonstrate shelter availability before enforcing neutral public conduct regulations goes well beyond what any reasonable reading of that precedent, the text, or the original understanding can support.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: While my background as a public defender makes me deeply sympathetic to the plight of homeless individuals and the practical consequences of criminalizing survival behaviors, the Eighth Amendment's text and precedent do not support the Ninth Circuit's expansive reading. Robinson v. California, 370 U.S. 660 (1962), prohibited criminalizing the status of addiction, but Powell v. Texas, 392 U.S. 514 (1968), made clear that conduct — even conduct closely tied to a condition — may be regulated, and Ingraham v. Wright, 430 U.S. 651 (1977), confirms the Clause has historically been directed at modes of punishment rather than the substantive scope of criminal prohibitions. The Ninth Circuit's population-level shelter-availability inquiry creates an unworkable standard that effectively strips municipalities of any meaningful ability to manage public spaces, and the proper remedy for the homelessness crisis lies in legislative and executive action — including robust funding for shelter and housing — rather than constitutionalizing a judicially unmanageable limitation on neutral public-conduct ordinances. I write separately to emphasize that while the City prevails here, governments retain obligations under equal protection and due process doctrines, and enforcement of these ordinances in a discriminatory or grossly disproportionate manner remains subject to constitutional challenge.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Eighth Amendment's Cruel and Unusual Punishment Clause prohibits cities from enforcing anti-camping ordinances against homeless individuals when there is no available shelter space, as established in Martin v. City of Boise.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Eighth Amendment to the United States Constitution (Cruel and Unusual Punishment Clause), specifically its application to municipal anti-camping and public sleeping ordinances enforced against homeless individuals
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The City of Grants Pass argues that the Ninth Circuit's Martin-based framework improperly expands the Eighth Amendment beyond its original scope, unconstitutionally restricts local governments' ability to regulate public spaces and homeless encampments, creates an unworkable population-level inquiry that should at most be an individualized assessment, and conflicts with the California Supreme Court's interpretation of the same constitutional question, thereby creating an untenable legal conflict within the same jurisdiction requiring Supreme Court resolution
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that the Ninth Circuit correctly applied Eighth Amendment protections because the ordinances deliberately target a vulnerable socioeconomic class warranting strict scrutiny, criminalize innocent and necessary acts of survival such as sleeping, violate the Eighth Amendment's substantive limits on what conduct can be criminalized and punished, and are consistent with this Court's precedents in Robinson, Powell, and Weems which prohibit punishment of involuntary status or condition
key_precedents: Martin v. City of Boise, 920 F.3d 584 (9th Cir. 2019)
Tobe v. City of Santa Ana, 9 Cal. 4th 1069 (1995)
Auto Equity Sales, Inc. v. Superior Court, 57 Cal. 2d 450 (1962)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor's refinement — suggesting individualized rather than population-level shelter-availability findings — is the most constructive proposal from the respondent side, and I take seriously her point that workability concerns counsel refinement rather than abandonment of Robinson's animating principle. However, even an individualized inquiry would require federal courts to make real-time factual determinations about shelter availability in specific localities, creating ongoing constitutional litigation over municipal resource allocation that the Eighth Amendment's text and history simply do not contemplate. Justice Jackson's candor about the workability problems with Martin, combined with her acknowledgment that the framework needs refinement, actually reinforces my view that the Ninth Circuit's categorical population-level approach cannot stand. I would write narrowly — reversing on the specific population-level inquiry while expressly preserving Robinson's status-based core and leaving open whether a truly individualized showing of complete unavailability might present a different constitutional question — a holding narrow enough to command a strong majority while avoiding the sweeping pronouncements that would unnecessarily foreclose future cases.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor's argument that sleeping is a biological necessity inseparable from homelessness deserves serious engagement, but it ultimately proves too much — by that logic, virtually any conduct necessary for survival would be immunized from criminal regulation, a result wholly untethered from the Eighth Amendment's text and original public meaning. The founding-era understanding of 'cruel and unusual punishments' was directed at the mode and severity of punishment imposed after conviction, not at the substantive legislative power to define criminal conduct; as Justice Gorsuch correctly notes, the Martin framework manufactures a constitutional rule from Justice Fortas's four-Justice Powell dissent and Justice White's narrow concurrence dicta that no majority of this Court has ever endorsed. Justice Jackson's suggestion that the act/status distinction 'collapses' when conduct is physiologically compelled was precisely the argument the Powell plurality rejected, and accepting it would transform the Eighth Amendment into an open-ended substantive limit on legislative power indistinguishable from Lochner-era substantive due process — a result I cannot countenance under any defensible theory of constitutional interpretation. Robinson's narrow holding prohibiting punishment of pure status remains intact; extending it to conduct-based ordinances through a population-level shelter-availability inquiry has no grounding in constitutional text, history, or legitimate precedent, and I remain firmly with the Petitioner.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson present the most sympathetic version of the respondents' position — that sleeping is a biological necessity inseparable from homelessness, making enforcement of anti-camping ordinances tantamount to punishing status itself. But this argument proves too much: virtually any conduct can be characterized as 'involuntary' or 'necessary' given a person's circumstances, and Robinson's holding was deliberately narrow, confined to pure status (being an addict) rather than any act, however compelled. As Justice Thomas correctly notes, Powell v. Texas reinforced that the Eighth Amendment does not constitutionalize a broad involuntariness defense to conduct-based criminal laws — the plurality there refused to extend Robinson even to chronic alcoholism manifested in public drunkenness, a case far more sympathetic than the general regulation of public camping. The Ninth Circuit's population-level shelter-availability inquiry is not only untethered from any majority holding of this Court but creates precisely the kind of judicially unmanageable standard that transforms federal courts into ongoing supervisors of municipal housing policy — a role the Constitution assigns to elected governments, not Article III judges.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Kagan's workability concern remains the strongest challenge to my position, and I take seriously that the Martin framework's population-level shelter inquiry is genuinely unmanageable — but as Justice Jackson correctly identifies, an unworkable remedy calls for refinement, not abandonment of the constitutional principle Robinson established. My colleagues in the majority repeatedly invoke Powell v. Texas, but they overstate its holding: the Powell plurality's refusal to extend Robinson was itself a plurality, not a majority, and Justice White's controlling concurrence explicitly preserved the question of whether punishing conduct that is physically unavoidable would violate the Eighth Amendment — meaning the act/status line they invoke was never as firmly drawn as they suggest. Justice Thomas argues that accepting the biological necessity argument would transform the Eighth Amendment into a Lochner-style substantive limit, but Robinson itself was a substantive limit on legislative power, and the question is not whether any involuntary conduct is immunized but whether conduct that is the direct, unavoidable physical manifestation of an involuntary status — sleeping when one has no shelter — can be distinguished from the status itself. I would affirm on narrower grounds than the Ninth Circuit, requiring individualized findings that a specific defendant had no available shelter alternative rather than a population-level inquiry, which addresses the workability concern while preserving Robinson's animating principle that the state cannot punish what a person cannot help doing.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson's refinement — proposing individualized rather than population-level shelter-availability findings — is genuinely more workable than the Ninth Circuit's framework, and I credit them for engaging seriously with the administrability concern. However, even an individualized inquiry requires federal courts to make ongoing factual determinations about shelter availability, alternative locations, and the voluntariness of particular defendants' circumstances, which still transforms Eighth Amendment litigation into a species of social policy adjudication that Robinson's text and Powell's fractured holding never contemplated. Justice Jackson's point that Robinson itself departed from a purely methodological reading of the Clause is well-taken, but Robinson's departure was categorical and narrow — it prohibited punishing a *status* as a crime, full stop — and extending that logic to conduct, even through an individualized lens, requires endorsing a principle that no majority of this Court has ever adopted and that the Powell plurality expressly rejected. I remain persuaded that the status/conduct line, however uncomfortable at the margins, is the constitutionally defensible boundary, and that the appropriate response to the genuine human suffering underlying this case lies with legislatures and local governments rather than with federal courts wielding an open-ended Eighth Amendment mandate.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson make the most compelling case for the respondents by arguing that sleeping is a biological necessity inseparable from the status of homelessness, such that punishing it collapses the act/status distinction Robinson established. But this argument proves too much: virtually any conduct can be characterized as the inevitable expression of some underlying condition, and Robinson itself drew a sharp line at status precisely to avoid this slippery slope — a line the Powell plurality explicitly refused to erase. Justice Jackson's suggestion that the conduct/status distinction 'collapses' when conduct is physiologically compelled would effectively constitutionalize an involuntariness defense that four Justices in Powell rejected and no majority has ever endorsed, transforming the Eighth Amendment into a substantive due process-style limit on legislative power with no textual or historical foundation. I agree with Justice Barrett that Ingraham v. Wright confirms the Clause operates on the method and degree of punishment, not on the legislature's definitional authority over criminal conduct, and the Ninth Circuit's population-level shelter-availability inquiry is precisely the kind of judicially unmanageable standard that signals we have strayed far from the constitutional text.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson make the most compelling case for the respondents by arguing that sleeping is a biological necessity inseparable from the condition of homelessness, such that punishing it effectively punishes status rather than conduct. This is a serious argument that deserves direct engagement: Robinson's core holding was that California could not make the *status* of addiction a criminal offense, but the ordinances at issue here attach liability to *conduct* — camping and sleeping in public spaces — not to the status of being homeless itself. Justice Sotomayor's 'biological necessity' framing, while sympathetic, would logically immunize a vast range of conduct from criminal regulation whenever that conduct is compelled by one's circumstances, a principle the Powell plurality expressly rejected and one that would transform the Eighth Amendment into an open-ended substantive limit on legislative power with no principled stopping point. As I noted in my initial reasoning, and as Justice Kagan reinforces, the Martin framework's population-level shelter-availability inquiry is judicially unmanageable and constitutionalizes a complex policy question that federalism and democratic governance principles reserve to local and state authorities — the Court's institutional legitimacy is best served by maintaining a clear act/status line rather than wading into ongoing municipal policy disputes.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson present the most compelling case for the respondents, arguing that when sleeping outdoors is biologically unavoidable and no shelter exists, enforcement effectively punishes the status of homelessness rather than any genuinely voluntary conduct. This is a serious argument that deserves direct engagement: Robinson's holding was narrow and categorical — it prohibited punishing the *status* of being an addict, full stop — and the Powell plurality explicitly refused to extend that logic to conduct, even conduct that flows inevitably from a status condition. The act/status distinction, however imperfect at the margins, is the line this Court drew in Powell, and as Justice Gorsuch correctly notes, no majority of this Court has ever endorsed the Fortas-White synthesis the Ninth Circuit employed in Martin to manufacture a broader involuntariness defense. Furthermore, Justice Sotomayor's 'biological necessity' argument, while sympathetic, proves too much — it would effectively immunize from criminal regulation any conduct that is physiologically compelled, an open-ended principle untethered from the Eighth Amendment's text and original meaning that would transform federal courts into supervisors of municipal social policy in ways the Constitution does not contemplate.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Kagan's workability argument is the strongest challenge to my position, and I acknowledge that the Martin framework's population-level shelter inquiry is genuinely unmanageable — but as I noted in round one, an unworkable remedy calls for refinement, not abandonment of the constitutional principle Robinson established. Justice Thomas presses the originalist point most forcefully, arguing that Robinson's logic would transform the Eighth Amendment into Lochner-era substantive due process, but Robinson itself was a substantive departure from a purely methodological reading of the Clause, and the Court has never overruled it — my colleagues who invoke Powell must reckon with the fact that Justice White's controlling concurrence in that fractured decision expressly reserved the question of whether punishing conduct that is genuinely unavoidable violates the Eighth Amendment. Justice Barrett's argument that the act/status distinction is the line Powell drew is correct as far as it goes, but the question here is precisely whether that line holds when the 'act' is physiologically inseparable from the status and no alternative exists — I would affirm on the narrow individualized-inquiry ground Justice Sotomayor and I have articulated, requiring a showing that a specific individual had no access to shelter before enforcement, which addresses workability concerns while preserving Robinson's animating principle that the state cannot punish what a person cannot help being.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Ninth Circuit's Martin framework improperly extends Robinson v. California beyond its narrow holding prohibiting punishment of mere status, into the realm of conduct regulation that Powell v. Texas explicitly preserved for legislative bodies. The plurality in Powell made clear that criminal penalties attached to public behavior — even behavior symptomatic of a condition — do not violate the Eighth Amendment, and Justice White's narrower concurrence did not command a majority for a broader conduct-based protection. As a matter of judicial minimalism and institutional legitimacy, I am reluctant to constitutionalize what is fundamentally a complex policy question about homelessness and urban governance that is better resolved through democratic processes at the local and state level; the Eighth Amendment's Cruel and Unusual Punishment Clause was designed to constrain the severity of punishment, not to serve as a wholesale limitation on what conduct municipalities may regulate. Reversing Martin on narrow grounds — holding that the Eighth Amendment does not categorically bar enforcement of neutral anti-camping ordinances against homeless individuals based on a population-level shelter-availability inquiry — preserves Robinson's core status-based protection while restoring appropriate federalism principles and avoiding the unworkable judicial administration the Ninth Circuit's framework has produced.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The original public meaning of the Eighth Amendment's Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause, as confirmed by Ingraham v. Wright, 430 U.S. 651 (1977), was directed at the method or kind of punishment imposed for criminal violations, not at the substantive authority of legislatures to define the scope of criminal prohibitions. The Ninth Circuit's Martin framework improperly extends Robinson v. California beyond its narrow holding — which prohibited criminalizing pure status such as drug addiction — to encompass conduct-based ordinances regulating public camping and sleeping, which are plainly acts of conduct, not immutable status. Robinson itself drew a sharp distinction between status and conduct, and Powell v. Texas, 392 U.S. 514 (1968), reinforced that the Eighth Amendment does not constitutionalize a broad involuntariness defense to conduct-based criminal laws; the Ninth Circuit's population-level shelter-availability inquiry has no grounding in the constitutional text, founding-era history, or any legitimate precedent of this Court. Consistent with principles of federalism and limited federal judicial power, municipalities retain the sovereign authority to regulate public spaces through generally applicable ordinances, and federal courts have no warrant under the Eighth Amendment to second-guess those legislative judgments.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Eighth Amendment's text and history confine the Cruel and Unusual Punishment Clause to regulating modes of punishment, not substantive limits on what conduct a legislature may criminalize beyond the narrow status-crime exception recognized in Robinson v. California. The Ninth Circuit's Martin framework improperly extended Robinson by treating involuntary conduct as equivalent to pure status, a move the Powell plurality expressly rejected when it refused to extend Robinson to acts that are 'in some sense involuntary,' and Justice White's controlling concurrence under the Marks rule supports only the narrow proposition that voluntary public conduct may be punished. Enforcing anti-camping ordinances against individuals who sleep in public constitutes regulation of conduct, not punishment of the mere status of being homeless, and the Ninth Circuit's population-level shelter-availability inquiry is judicially unmanageable, intrudes on local police powers, and finds no support in the Amendment's original meaning or this Court's precedents. Practical consequences reinforce this conclusion: the Martin rule has hamstrung municipalities across the Ninth Circuit from addressing genuine public health and safety concerns in shared public spaces, a result neither the text nor tradition of the Eighth Amendment requires.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Robinson v. California established that the Eighth Amendment prohibits criminalizing a person's status, and when homeless individuals have no access to shelter, enforcing anti-camping ordinances against them effectively punishes the involuntary condition of homelessness itself — a status, not a freely chosen act. The practical reality that sleeping is a biological necessity inseparable from the condition of homelessness means that, absent available shelter, these ordinances criminalize existence itself, precisely the kind of cruel and unusual punishment Robinson was designed to prevent. While Powell v. Texas drew a line at punishing conduct rather than status, the plurality's fractured reasoning should not be read to permit cities to punish the unavoidable physical acts that are the direct and inescapable consequence of an involuntary status, particularly when enforcement falls overwhelmingly on one of society's most vulnerable populations with nowhere else to turn. The Ninth Circuit's Martin framework, requiring only that shelter be unavailable before the Eighth Amendment protection attaches, strikes a measured and workable balance that respects both local regulatory authority and the constitutional floor against punishing involuntary human conditions.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Eighth Amendment's Cruel and Unusual Punishment Clause, as interpreted in Robinson v. California and the fractured Powell v. Texas decision, prohibits punishment of mere status but does not extend to conduct — even conduct that may be involuntary or compelled by one's condition. The Ninth Circuit's Martin framework improperly collapses this act/status distinction by effectively immunizing conduct (public camping, sleeping) based on a population-level inquiry into shelter availability, which neither Robinson's holding nor Justice White's narrow Powell concurrence supports. As a pragmatic matter, the Martin rule creates serious workability problems: it requires courts to make real-time assessments of shelter capacity across entire municipalities, invites inconsistent enforcement, and strips local governments of reasonable regulatory authority over public spaces without a firm constitutional foundation. The California Supreme Court's contrary analysis in Tobe v. City of Santa Ana correctly identifies that Robinson and Powell do not prohibit criminalization of acts merely derivative of a person's status, and that workable line — status versus conduct — should govern here.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: As a textualist and originalist, I must examine what the Eighth Amendment's Cruel and Unusual Punishment Clause actually prohibits based on its original meaning and text: it constrains the *manner* and *degree* of punishment imposed after a lawful conviction, not the substantive scope of what legislatures may criminalize. Robinson v. California, even accepting its contested holding, prohibited punishing the mere *status* of being an addict — a narrow ruling that the fractured Powell Court declined to extend to conduct, however involuntary. The Ninth Circuit's Martin framework improperly stitches together Justice Fortas's four-Justice dissent in Powell with Justice White's narrow concurrence dicta to manufacture a constitutional rule that no majority of this Court has ever endorsed, in violation of basic principles of precedent and constitutional interpretation. Furthermore, the separation of powers concern is acute here: allowing federal courts to override municipal public-order ordinances based on a population-level shelter-availability inquiry transforms the Eighth Amendment into an open-ended substantive due process-style limit on legislative power, precisely the kind of judicial policymaking that the Constitution reserves to elected governments.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Ninth Circuit's Martin framework represents an unworkable and historically unsupported extension of the Eighth Amendment beyond its original scope as a constraint on punishments rather than a limit on what conduct legislatures may criminalize. Powell v. Texas, 392 U.S. 514 (1968), failed to produce a majority opinion and thus provides no binding precedent for extending Robinson's narrow status-based holding to conduct, however involuntary that conduct may be; the plurality explicitly warned against extending Robinson 'by even a fraction of an inch.' The practical workability concerns are severe — a population-level inquiry into available shelter capacity creates an unmanageable standard that strips local governments of their traditional police power to regulate public spaces, a power deeply rooted in history and tradition. As an institutionalist matter, the Court should be cautious about constitutionalizing what is fundamentally a complex policy question best resolved through democratic processes at the local and state level, consistent with our precedents in Ingraham v. Wright limiting the Eighth Amendment's reach to the criminal punishment context.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: As an originalist and textualist, I must examine what 'cruel and unusual punishment' meant at the time of the Eighth Amendment's ratification, and nothing in that historical record suggests the Clause was understood to restrict the substantive scope of what conduct legislatures may criminalize beyond the narrow status-based holding of Robinson v. California. Robinson's holding is properly cabined to prohibiting punishment of pure status — being an addict — and the Powell plurality correctly refused to extend that principle to conduct, even involuntary conduct flowing from status; the Ninth Circuit's Martin framework improperly stitches together Justice Fortas's dissent and Justice White's narrow concurrence to manufacture a constitutional rule that no majority of this Court has ever endorsed. Furthermore, Ingraham v. Wright explicitly clarified that the Eighth Amendment 'was designed to protect those convicted of crimes' and operates as a limitation on punishment's method and degree, not as a substantive limit on legislative power to define criminal conduct — meaning cities retain authority to regulate public spaces through anti-camping ordinances without Eighth Amendment constraint. The Martin framework also creates an unworkable population-level inquiry untethered from individualized criminal adjudication, conflicts with the California Supreme Court's reasoning in Tobe v. City of Santa Ana, and improperly conscripts federal courts into supervising local policy choices that the Constitution leaves to democratic governance.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Drawing on Robinson v. California's core principle that the Eighth Amendment prohibits criminalizing involuntary status or conditions, I find that enforcing anti-camping ordinances against homeless individuals when no shelter space exists effectively punishes the unavoidable consequence of their condition — homelessness itself — rather than any genuinely voluntary conduct. While Powell v. Texas drew a line at criminalizing conduct versus status, the practical reality here, informed by my background as a public defender, is that sleeping outdoors when no indoor alternative exists is no more a voluntary 'act' than addiction was a voluntary 'status' in Robinson; the distinction collapses when the conduct is the only physiological option available. The procedural fairness concern is acute: imposing criminal penalties on individuals who have no meaningful choice transforms the justice system into an instrument of punishment for poverty rather than deterrence of genuine wrongdoing, undermining equal protection principles. I would affirm the Ninth Circuit's framework in Martin, though I would clarify that the Eighth Amendment inquiry must account for individualized circumstances and the actual availability of shelter, rather than a purely population-level assessment, to preserve workable enforcement standards for municipalities.
